algebra.description: Solving linear equations in one variable.
Solving linear inequalities in one variable and interpreting their solution sets.
Understanding and calculating the slope and y-intercept of linear equations.
Graphing linear equations on the coordinate plane and analyzing their graphs.
Understanding parallel and perpendicular lines and their relationships (slopes).
Solving systems of linear equations in two variables.
Solving or graphing systems of linear inequalities in two variables.
Using linear equations to solve real-world word problems.
Solving word problems by setting up and solving systems of equations.
Rearranging algebraic formulas to solve for a given variable.
Modeling and solving real-world scenarios using inequalities.
Solving mixture (solution/combination) problems using linear equations.
Solving motion problems using the relationship distance = rate × time.
Working with direct proportional relationships (y = kx) and their properties.
Solving age-related word problems with linear equations.

advanced-math.description: Solving equations that contain absolute value expressions.
Solving inequalities involving absolute value expressions.
Solving quadratic equations by factoring, quadratic formula, etc.
Factoring polynomial expressions into simpler factors.
Expanding products of polynomials into standard form.
Simplifying rational expressions by factoring and reducing fractions.
Solving equations that involve rational expressions (fractions).
Solving equations that include radical expressions (e.g., square roots).
Applying laws of exponents to simplify or manipulate expressions.
Solving equations where the variable appears in the exponent.
Solving problems involving exponential growth or decay.
Understanding and using function notation (f(x)) and evaluating functions.
Forming and evaluating compositions of functions (f(g(x))).
Solving systems of equations where at least one equation is nonlinear.

problem-solving-and-data-analysis.description: Solving problems involving ratios, proportions, and direct variation.
Converting between different units or rates.
Calculating percentages, percentage changes, and related problems.
Calculating and understanding mean, median, and other measures of center.
Understanding measures of spread (range, standard deviation conceptually).
Interpreting one-variable data distributions (e.g., from charts or lists of data).
Analyzing scatterplots to understand relationships between two variables.
Interpreting or using the line of best fit in a scatterplot.
Calculating probabilities given a condition or using two-way tables.
Analyzing two-way tables for frequencies, probabilities, or relationships.
Understanding random sampling and how it affects data and conclusions.
Understanding experimental vs. observational studies and control vs. treatment groups.
Interpreting the margin of error in surveys or polls and what it implies.
Drawing conclusions about a population based on sample data.

geometry-and-trigonometry.description: Calculating area of basic polygons (triangles, rectangles, etc.).
Finding angles formed by intersecting or parallel lines (e.g., vertical angles, corresponding angles).
Using properties of triangle angles (sum of interior angles is 180°, exterior angles).
Solving problems using similar triangles and proportional side lengths.
Using sine, cosine, or tangent in right triangles to find unknown sides or angles.
Calculating volumes of 3D shapes (prisms, cylinders, spheres, etc.).
Using the distance formula and midpoint formula in the coordinate plane.
Applying a² + b² = c² to find a missing side in a right triangle.
Using properties of 45-45-90 or 30-60-90 triangles to find side lengths.
Calculating interior or exterior angle sums for polygons.
Calculating circumference and area of circles; understanding radius and diameter.
Working with arcs, central angles, and inscribed angles in circle problems.
Using the equation of a circle (center-radius form) and identifying circle parameters.
Calculating surface area of 3D objects (prisms, cylinders, spheres, etc.).

craft-and-structure.description: Determining the meaning of a specific word based on its context in the passage.
Interpreting the meaning of a phrase or idiom as used in context.
Understanding metaphors, similes, or other figurative expressions in the text.
Analyzing how the author’s word choice influences meaning or tone.
Identifying how the passage is organized (chronological, compare-contrast, etc.).
Determining the author’s primary purpose or goal in the passage.
Recognizing the author’s tone or mood (e.g., sarcastic, formal, optimistic).
Understanding the author’s attitude or viewpoint toward the subject.
Identifying the perspective from which the passage is told (first person, third person, etc.).
Determining the function of a specific sentence or detail in the passage.
Recognizing rhetorical techniques (examples, anecdotes, rhetorical questions) used by the author.
Understanding how the author structures their argument or reasoning.
Comparing and contrasting ideas or viewpoints between two passages.
Drawing a conclusion or connection using information from two related passages.
Inferring the intended audience or readership for the passage.

information-and-ideas.description: Identifying the central idea or primary claim of the passage.
Finding specific details or facts stated explicitly in the passage.
Inferring information that is implied but not directly stated in the passage.
Choosing the piece of text that best supports a given statement or answer.
Interpreting information from a graph or table that accompanies the passage.
Understanding cause-and-effect relationships described in the passage.
Identifying similarities or differences between ideas or events in the passage.
Selecting a sentence that logically completes or continues the passage.
Drawing a logical conclusion from the information presented in the passage.
Determining the author’s position or opinion on the topic discussed.
Applying the passage’s ideas or logic to a new hypothetical scenario or question.
Identifying a specific claim or argument made in the passage.
Determining the main idea or purpose of a particular paragraph in the passage.
Choosing a title or summary that best reflects the passage’s main idea.
Identifying information or statements that are not supported by the passage.

standard-english-conventions.description: Ensuring the subject and verb agree in number (singular vs. plural).
Using correct and consistent verb tenses in context.
Making sure pronouns clearly refer to the correct noun and agree in number.
Using the correct pronoun case (e.g., I vs. me, who vs. whom).
Using a consistent grammatical structure for items in a list or comparison.
Placing modifiers correctly to avoid ambiguity (no dangling or misplaced modifiers).
Making logical comparisons without leaving words or ideas out (comparing like terms).
Using commas correctly (in lists, after clauses) and avoiding comma splices.
Using semicolons and colons correctly to join clauses or introduce lists.
Using apostrophes correctly for possessives and contractions.
Avoiding sentence fragments by ensuring each sentence is complete.
Avoiding run-on sentences or comma splices by properly separating clauses.
Using the correct prepositions or expressions in standard idioms.
Avoiding commonly confused or misused words (e.g., affect vs. effect).
Using adjectives and adverbs correctly (e.g., good vs. well).

expression-of-ideas.description: Removing redundant words or phrases to be more concise.
Revising text to eliminate ambiguity or confusion for clearer meaning.
Choosing the most precise and appropriate words to convey the idea.
Maintaining a consistent tone and style appropriate to the passage.
Ensuring all content is on-topic (adding relevant details or deleting off-topic ones).
Adding examples, facts, or details to better support a claim or idea.
Providing a clear topic sentence or introduction to introduce the main idea.
Giving an effective concluding sentence or summary to wrap up a discussion.
Arranging sentences and ideas in a logical order to improve flow.
Using transition words or phrases to smoothly connect ideas.
Combining sentences or clauses to improve flow and avoid repetition.
Organizing information within a paragraph in the clearest, most logical way.
Incorporating additional information (like data or notes) smoothly into the text.
Using active voice for clarity and directness when appropriate.
Ensuring the language maintains an appropriate level of formality.
